Scalability

SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 15

Given February 23rd, 2025 by Yonatan Stern



So I'm pretty surprised that we are on lecture number 15. And I got from a few people here that they say, "Don't stop, keep coming up with things." I said I start repeating myself. They said, "That's good, because at my age I don't remember anything anyway." So I'll probably just repeat myself. The subject of this lecture is, kind of surprisingly, scalability. And the reason I'm bringing scalability up, as you will see amply in the presentation, is because this is one of those keywords that venture capital firms use all the time. So I thought it would be useful to analyze what scalability means — is it good, is it bad, and what does it do? But as usual, I'll start with what is SmartUp. And that's myself. Ayala is sitting there and Libby, who is running the whole thing.



I want to introduce what SmartUp is slightly differently this time. So the common knowledge or idea is that 9 out of 10 startups fail — or as VCs say, 1 out of 10 succeeds — and when it succeeds, it returns all the money. And we are very excited, and they kind of gloss over the fact that 9 out of 10 founders fail, which I think is a devastating statistic. So the purpose of SmartUp is that you can succeed. That's really the purpose. If we talk about it in one word, this is it. Now, what is success? We define success as three things. Number one, that the company is profitable — but really profitable, not one month yes, one month no, but profitable every month. Number two, that it's fast growing, that this is not a lifestyle business where you're making just enough money to spend your time in Hawaii. And number three, that it requires a modest investment, so you don't have to pour in $100 million before you reach profitability. That's our definition of a successful company. And our objective is to increase the success rate. So if the success rate today is 1 in 10, we would like to get to 1 in 2, maybe 1 in 3. We don't know — that's why we are working with companies, because we want to verify that this is actually doable, that we can increase the success rate significantly by following certain methods and principles.

And what is a modest investment? I've been thinking a lot about it. I think it's somewhere between $2 million and $5 million, depending on the company and what needs to be done — but definitely not the $30 to $50 million that VCs talk about. We've discussed a lot about why VCs do what they do. I won't go into that right now.

What is the infinite gain? Keep talking about the vision of SmartUp — if we increase the success rate from 1 out of 10 to 1 out of 5, 1 out of 3, or maybe 1 out of 2, that's a multiplication by 3 or maybe 5, so it's a major multiplier. And if we reduce the investment required by a factor of 3, or maybe 5 — we're actually talking about reducing it by a factor of 10 — but let's just say a factor of 3. That means you and us together can grow the startup industry by a factor of 10. Not 10% — a factor of 10. I think that's a vision and an infinite game that is worth pursuing, which is why I do this. And we can have 10 times as many successful entrepreneurs — all of you. Look around: there are 10 people here. I made sure that if we want to have 10 successful entrepreneurs, they are right here, all of them. And I'm serious about it.

One of the things I think is very painful is that people who fail think they are idiots and failures, and they leave the pursuit. Because you have to be really strong to fail at something, and then come back and say, "No, I can do it again, and this time I'm wiser." Most people will just give up and move on. And these are exactly the right people to keep going, because they already know what not to do. So it's very important.

So what is the SmartUp Academy? It's a program to teach the engineering profession of building a company. I show people a lot of things about what it means to build a company. And now I can say it's 15 lectures — next time I write it, it'll probably say 16. These lectures cover all the aspects of building a company, from branding to marketing, sales, product pricing, packaging, how to recruit people — you name it. They're all part of what we try to show, teach, and explain in the context of startups. These things behave differently when you are a big company. But when you are a startup, there are some very simple rules you should be following.

Obviously, the jewel in the crown is the residency program — very much like the picture here shows. If you want to be a doctor, it's not enough to be on the dean's list after six years of school. You really need to spend a few years in a hospital, work with real patients and doctors, and understand what you're doing. Same goes for here. Right now we work with about seven companies, and we learn a lot from it — and I hope they learn a lot from it.

Okay, so what are scalable business models? Venture capital firms prefer to invest in companies that have a scalable business model. It's a term. What is a scalable business model? Basically, it means that you can multiply your revenues without multiplying your costs. I've talked about it before. You want to be in a situation where when you start growing, your growth is not linear with your inputs — so if you want to grow twice as much, you don't have to put in twice as many resources.

But that's not really the problem. The problem is the next item: VCs don't like non-scalable business models. Actually, they don't like anything that has the feeling of being non-scalable. So the entire lecture today, the entire analysis, will be around that line — which is why it's highlighted.

I heard it too many times from people and from VCs: "This is not scalable." Let me tell you a story. I won't say the names because I didn't ask permission. But one of the angel investors we deal with came in with a company he had invested in — he's the active chairman — and he wanted our opinion and insights. What the company does is they have a software that simulates the processes of growing bacteria and yeast. Why do they want to grow bacteria and yeast? Because nowadays these are factories for all kinds of chemicals, like insulin and other molecules. They modify the yeast or the bacteria, and then they need to grow it in an incubator. It turns out this is a very delicate and sophisticated process. Each experiment or round of improvement takes weeks, months, and costs a lot of money. So they built a simulator where they can run the experiment virtually before running it in real life. Obviously the simulator is just — push a button and you get the simulation.

So I looked at it, and it took a while for them to explain it to me. I'm open-minded, and I think I got the point. And I told him: "I trust that most people you go to will not understand what you're doing. And if they understand, they won't believe you, because it looks like magic. And honestly, I think your idea is great, but it will require a lot of iterations before you really get a simulation that works."

So he said, "Okay, what should we do?" I said it's pretty simple. Instead of selling the software, you should sell the output of the software. So if a customer wants to run an experiment, you talk to them and say, "We expect that this experiment, if it works, will increase productivity by 10%. We ran it in our simulation and we believe we can change the recipe to get to 17%." So you tell them, "I believe we can get you to 12%. And if we do, we charge you $10,000, plus $2,000 for every percentage point above 12." Then the customer takes no risk — because if you don't reach 12%, they pay nothing, which is in line with what they already expected, which was 10%. And then all the knowledge stays in your hands, and you're the only ones touching the machine, so it doesn't really have to work perfectly because you're going to fix it anyway.

And then the angel investor said something that really floored me. He said, "This is not scalable — we won't be able to raise money." I said, "Why is it not scalable?" He said, "Only SaaS is scalable. This is not scalable." Honestly, I was shocked. He's a very sophisticated guy who made a lot of money in many ventures, and he truly believed that if you're not selling software but instead selling the results of the software, it is not scalable.

That's what made me decide we're going to discuss scalability today. Because I think this is a huge missed opportunity for many companies — it's driving them into a lot of trouble, as I will show with one of our portfolio companies. And it's a waste.

What are non-scalable models? If we talk about scalable, what is the non-scalable model? It's basically anything that involves people. Look around you — we are not scalable. Actually, each and every one of us is a whole world, as we say. And when we are the whole world, that means a lot of complexity. You know my opinion about companies — keep it down to just you, if you can. If you have no choice, bring in your spouse.

Keeping it down to just yourself is not scalable, basically. But in reality, everything that involves consulting, services, training — whatever requires people — in the mind of VCs is not scalable, and they will not invest in a company that has non-scalable elements. One of the companies — I don't know where he is, he gave me his materials but he's not here today — when they arrived, he mentioned something to a VC, and the VC said, "Never say that word again" — I'll talk about what the word was later — "because this is not scalable, we're not going to invest in you." So this seems to be a very important word for VCs.

And since many of us do talk to VCs, I wanted to discuss it.

So what do scalability and growth engines have to do with one another? If you look at when I presented it in lecture number seven, I basically say the same thing. A growth engine is a process that the company does — or plans to do — many times, repeatedly, in marketing, in sales, or in any other critical activity. It's a scalable process — you can double its output with a small increase in input, and it's not linear: a small increase in input can yield a large increase in output. What's the difference? It's essentially the same exact definition. So probably we're missing something.

So I thought a lot about what the difference actually is — and here it is. What VCs mean by scalable, and what I mean by a growth engine, are two very different concepts. Venture capital scalable business models are basically generic business models — which I will show in a moment — that can scale well if implemented properly. That means if you follow those models, they can literally grow like a rocket ship. You've all seen them before, and many of you will recognize the names I bring up. Yes, there are several business models that are scalable, and there are many well-known companies that used them to grow into big companies. That's what VCs mean.
Mented properly. That means if you follow those models, they can literally grow like this. You know all of those things. You have seen them before, right? Many of you will recognize the names I bring. So yes, there are several business models that are scalable, and there are many well-known companies that use them to grow into big companies. So that's what VCs mean.

And the only problem is — and I will show it later on — is that these business models require a lot of investment upfront and a bit of luck, or a lot of luck, because a lot of people try to do them and it's usually one winner. That's about it. So you need a good amount of luck in order to succeed in building that. And as you know, if I want to bring the success rate from 1 out of 10 to 1 out of 2, luck is not what we want to take into account. We want it to be a far more repeatable business. So if that is what VCs mean, what do we mean? We mean us. So when I thought about growth engines, I thought about three different problems that we are trying to solve.

The first one — we spent two lectures talking about branding and marketing. Notice the first word: how to ignite growth from zero. So all the models that I showed you in those two lectures, the whole idea was that you can start them from zero with no investment, or very little investment, which is very different from what we're going to see with what VCs do. The whole idea there is you can start building a brand and marketing and do that with relatively little investment. The idea was to choose the ones that will continue to grow as you grow. The second, which is the main thing I want to talk about today, is how to introduce a new product concept to the market. The last item is overcoming what is usually a non-scalable process.

Let me give you an example. If you look at Wolt — so what Wolt did is they built a whole service with thousands of people that ride scooters on the street. Every time I go to Tel Aviv, I get a heart attack. Somehow not all of them die — I don't know how they do it — but they are not Wolt employees. They are independent contractors. They're called partners, I think that's the term they use. So Wolt can grow as much as they want because they don't have any fixed cost of employment. So that's kind of a scalable business model. But I want to show others that apply to other things. So these are the three things. Let's go back to what the VCs talk about.

So what is a scalable business model? The most famous one is what's called the marketplace or platform model. And they go by industry. So let's start with services and labor markets. Fiverr — scalable business model. You build the platform, people list their skills, people look up others with those skills, talk to them, contract them. Fiverr is just the platform; it doesn't do anything itself. But there are many of them — Upwork, it's freelancers; TaskRabbit. TaskRabbit is the most hands-on of them. In July I went with the family to Boston because I have an apartment there and I needed to clean it and take everything back to Israel. So we had about 12 suitcases that I needed to move and we live on the third floor. And I was scratching my head because I was not planning on taking 12 suitcases — I have only girls, okay — and there's no elevator. So my daughter said, "What's the problem? Use TaskRabbit." I said, "What the hell is TaskRabbit?" TaskRabbit is exactly that. People. You want them to do some dirty job and you're willing to pay them by the hour. So I went on TaskRabbit. They have this funny thing where all the prices are like $44.44 per hour — I don't know why they do that, it's kind of one of their jokes. And so I found a guy and I said, "I need you to come on this day, at this hour, you have to take 12 suitcases down the stairs, put them in the car, and drive with us to the airport so we can take them out of the car and go stand in line." He agreed and he came, and I talked to him.

It turns out that he's doing his master's degree in physics at MIT. So he was the best schlepper I ever had, with a degree. But it works. I paid him, I don't know, $200 or whatever, and I didn't break my back. And there's Care.com for babysitters, and Rover for pet sitting and dog walking, and so on. Doordash is the Wolt of America — and Wolt is also here. So this is a scalable marketplace platform. And there are many others. Same goes for transportation and mobility — Uber, we all know, is ride-sharing. Gett, which is basically a taxi dispatcher. Lyft, which is a competitor of Uber. Bird and Lime for scooters — anybody knows them here? And Blablacar is my favorite. With a name like Blablacar, what can go wrong?

And obviously we have commerce — eBay, all of us know it. Craigslist. People here know what Craigslist is? If I were you, I wouldn't nod my head because it shows how old you are. The new generation has no idea what Craigslist is. Craigslist is the original — before all of that stuff, the UI was just text. I think it's still just text. I haven't been there in a long time. Okay, I think you get the point.

Now, what are the strengths and weaknesses of these business models? That's really the important thing. Let's start with the strengths, and let's talk about the model and then the market. The first one is they solve a real problem. That's a strength. They connect and coordinate between suppliers and customers of services of all kinds. They basically do this connection.

Second, they have the benefit of the network effect. Network effect means every customer brings another customer. More suppliers attract more customers, who attract more suppliers. So it starts to expand really rapidly. And that's exactly why it is scalable — because the more business you do, the more business you do. The growth by network effects creates defensibility. What does that mean? It's going to be tremendously difficult for a company to compete with Wolt in Israel, right? Because once they get in and reach a certain level, nobody's going to build another auction site like eBay, because eBay already controls the market. So as you grow, the moment you get to a certain size, you basically dominate the market and you don't have competition anymore. And they reduce transaction friction and build trust.

Many times the question is — like with eBay, you pay but you haven't received the product yet. So you have to trust that you're going to get the product, or your money back. So the platform is often the intermediary that guarantees the transaction is going to happen. And if not, they still have the money and they'll give it back to you. That's a very important element. And also they can create liquidity even if they don't control the entire market. So TaskRabbit is focusing on a very narrow part of the market and can reach enough power and enough size to be viable, even though they don't control all the work of all consultants and everybody.

You'll see that a lot of these platforms are very specific to very specific tasks or geographic locations. Wolt is a Finnish company, I think — they're in Israel, in Holland. So what else? Cost benefits. Providers handle delivery and service. eBay doesn't do anything — it's the person who wants to sell who takes your money, then packs it and ships it to you. So all the platform does is handle the matching and the money. That's a tremendous benefit. They make money as a percentage of each transaction — all of these do. So every transaction they take a cut, anywhere between 5% and 30%, and maybe even more. And they also have strong unit economics. Once scale is achieved, once you get to enough revenue, then everything else is on top of it.

Once you've paid for all your costs — and this is what's beautiful about these scalable models — once you've paid for the servers and the developers and everything else, then every dollar above that is pure profit. That's really nice.

So those are the strengths and benefits. But what about the weaknesses? Well, there's a problem. There's a chicken-and-egg problem. You open a website and you say, "List your whatever on this website" — but nobody's ever heard about it, so nobody's going to put anything on it. To ignite — remember I said before, when we talked about branding and marketing, we talked about igniting growth — to ignite a platform like that is very difficult. Now you start to understand why I said it requires a lot of money and luck.

Because you start with an empty thing and you need to start building it very rapidly. It often requires subsidies on both sides. So Uber — why did Uber raise so much money? I mean, if everything is so great, why do you need so much money? Well, the answer is there's a nasty secret. If they launch Uber in Tel Aviv and you open the app and look for drivers and there are none, you will not use it anymore. If you get disappointed once or twice, that's it. You're never going to look at it again. So they have to make sure they have enough drivers waiting for your call. But the drivers don't want to be there because there are no customers.

So what Uber did is, whenever they wanted to penetrate a new city, they hired thousands of drivers and paid them to just sit there waiting. They had to do it for weeks and months, so that whenever a customer wanted a ride, there was a ride available — not an hour from now, but right now. Because people are impatient; they want a ride right now. That's why they needed huge amounts of money in order to launch city by city. And in each city you start from scratch because it's the same problem every time. There are some hidden secrets to all of these phenomenal business models that people don't talk about. So it can be very expensive.

There's another problem. If you have a seller who wants to sell something on eBay and is going to lose 20% or 30% of the transaction to eBay itself — that, by the way, is what happens with apps. If you put your application on the App Store or on Google Play, once you reach a certain level, you have to pay 30% of the transaction to Google or Apple. 30% is a lot of money just to be on the platform. There's poor economics there, and that can create a lot of issues, because usually the people who pay for it are the vendors, not the customers. So it's not all nice and easy with all of these scalable business models. In order to ignite them, many are actually buying revenue through subsidies. That's what happens.

Okay, let's move on to another very famous one — PLG, Product-Led Growth. If you talk to a lot of entrepreneurs, they have this vision that the product will sell itself. It's such a great product and it's going to just work. So let's look at it. Collaboration and productivity — for those of you who know Slack, the messaging app; Zoom, which we're using right now to record this session; Discord for communication; Figma, Canva, and so on. All of them have the same concept. It's free for individual users and you upgrade to enterprise, which costs money. So if you want to use it as a company, you have to pay. Which immediately raises the question — how do you know what is an individual user using it for free, and how do you know it's a company that can pay? And how do you enforce that?
Meeting. Discord, communication, Figma, Canva, and so on. All of them have the same concept. It's free for individual users and you upgrade to enterprise — that costs you money. So if you want to use it as a company, you have to pay. Which immediately brings the question: how do you know what is an individual user using it for free, and how do you know that it's a company that can pay? How do you do that?

I won't tell you. Another category is sales and marketing: Calendly, Mailchimp — all of you know HubSpot, SurveyMonkey. All of them have the same business model of product-led growth. Same thing. GitHub — just to remind you, they were acquired by Microsoft for $7.5 billion back in 2019 — so it works if you're the lucky one. MongoDB, GitLab, and all of that stuff.

Let's look at the strengths and weaknesses. Lower customer acquisition cost, right? Because most of the growth happens by word of mouth. That's the way these models work. You have a really good product, people start talking about it, people start using it, other people hear about it, and it starts to grow. The users usually find the product themselves — it's kind of magic. Well, not entirely by themselves.

If I've used Zoom and I really like it and I want to talk to you, I'll tell you: "Zvika, use Zoom, it's good." Because I want to talk to you — same with WhatsApp, all of these applications. Anyway, you see why communication apps are heavily represented here, because they inherently create the network effect. They spread within organizations. So if I start using Zoom in my organization and I start setting up meetings on Zoom, then everybody else is going to use Zoom for meetings — and that's how it spreads.

And it's very easy to spot upsell opportunities. LinkedIn used to do it a lot. If LinkedIn saw that people started using the Sales Navigator — one user, you just put in your credit card; two users, you put in your credit card; but then you get a call from a salesperson saying, "I see that your company has at least three users — we have a package for you." I remember getting that at Zoom and at other companies. They have a very simple system: they track how many users from each company, and once it reaches a certain threshold, you get a phone call from a salesperson. Very simple.

Now, that's a whole different discussion — I won't go into it. And the interesting thing here is that it creates two dynamics: bottom-up adoption that leads to top-down purchase. So people use it within the company — either for free, or they put in their personal credit card. And then when it reaches a certain level of usage inside the company, higher-level management says, "No, no, we need to standardize, we need to do this correctly — let's make sure it's an enterprise-level product, that it doesn't introduce security issues," and so on. So it starts to become a top-down discussion.

The pricing is also very interesting. Even when I got a call from LinkedIn for Sales Navigator, they still sold packages by number of users. Zoom did the same. Think about it — when you have an organization with people using the product internally, and you want to turn it into an enterprise deal, the enterprise deal is still typically priced by number of users. So it gives you a tremendous opportunity: five people in a company of 500 are using it, and suddenly you have the opportunity to sell 500 licenses — or 100 licenses, depending on what the product does. So it's a highly attractive business model. VCs are not stupid — these are really good business models.

What are the weaknesses? They're kind of nasty, and they're subtle. The product must be at a very high quality from the start. You can't launch a broken product that works sometimes and crashes all the time — it just doesn't work. So you have to invest a good amount of money to polish the product before you put it out in the market, because otherwise you're going to ruin your brand. You have to come in with a very big upfront investment in the product.

And that's why I started with the question: what is the purpose of our startup? When I talk about small investment, these kinds of business models immediately signal that I'm not sure you can really get to success with $2 million — it's just too risky. You're not going to make it on that. So you clearly start to see that if you want to succeed with a high probability, the business models you want to pursue look different from these ones.

As I said before, the transition from free to paying is not trivial. I used the words "artistry," "ingenuity," and "imagination." What does that mean? People love free products. They hate it when you suddenly say, "Now you have to pay for something you used for free." We get used to free products very quickly — you get addicted to them. If Google started charging $10 a month — or even YouTube. How many people pay for YouTube to remove ads? A tiny fraction. Why? Because it's free. It just is.

It happened to Microsoft with Hotmail, right? Remember Hotmail? 50 megabytes free. And why is email free? Because the people who started it gave it away for free. Think about it this way — when I started out, you paid per minute on a phone call, right? Nobody pays per minute anymore. It's unlimited. Why? Because the cost came down enough that carriers could afford it, and competition forced them to offer unlimited plans.

Same goes for Internet usage — we pay a flat fee. And there's a huge argument in the US about net neutrality. Have you ever heard about net neutrality? No? Shame on you. Net neutrality is the question of who pays for Internet service. You think you pay for Internet service — but that's not entirely true. Because when you sit and watch Netflix around the clock, who's paying for that traffic? Not you, and not Netflix directly. The people who wanted to change it are the carriers — the ones who actually move the traffic. They argued that the huge users like Netflix, Amazon, Disney — all the companies that stream massive amounts of content — should pay for the access to the infrastructure. These roughly ten companies account for something like 70% of Internet traffic — it's staggering.

When the Internet started, they established this concept of net neutrality: you don't interfere with what's going on in the network. That's it — we're neutral. And there's been a huge ongoing fight about it. With Trump, things will probably change, because he follows the money. But you see that this is not simple — moving from free to paying is a very difficult thing to do.

I told you about my tremendous respect for Zoom for coming up with this great idea: 40 minutes free, then it disconnects. Which immediately, if you're running a business meeting, makes you raise your hand — "No, no, I can't afford to look cheap, I'm going to pay." It's really smart. That's what I mean by ingenuity. People figure out clever ways to move you from personal use to business use, making the distinction very subtle. They don't come out and say, "If you're a business, you have to pay." Zoom doesn't say that. And then there's WhatsApp for Business — it costs a lot of money, and it's growing like crazy.

The other problem is that you need a very large user base to generate meaningful revenue. What do I mean? Because the conversion rate from free to paying is relatively low — for every paying customer, you have roughly 100 non-paying customers. And those non-paying customers still use resources: servers, bandwidth, infrastructure. One question I was once asked: how much energy does your phone consume? Most people say, "Almost nothing — I just charge it at night." The answer is that a cell phone consumes about as much energy as a refrigerator. How? Because your phone is just the endpoint of a very long process. When you run Waze, there's a lot of computing happening behind the scenes — it starts on servers somewhere. All of those servers consume a lot of energy. So all of these "free" services are not actually free to run. It costs a lot of money.

So: big investment required to make the product enterprise-ready. If you want to move from consumer to enterprise, the product has to meet enterprise standards — it needs to be secure, scalable, and all the things that go along with that. Very, very important.

Now you're starting to see why all of these are really good, scalable business models — but with significant challenges. So let me tell you a story about LinkedIn. It was co-founded by Reid Hoffman and launched in May 2003. Who is Reid Hoffman? Prior to founding LinkedIn, he joined PayPal. The founders and top executives of PayPal basically went on to start many of the famous companies in Silicon Valley. He was Senior VP of Business Development and reported to the then-CEO of PayPal — you might have heard the name: Elon Musk. It's like musical chairs with all these people.

Before LinkedIn's IPO, they raised $155 million. Why do I tell you all of that? Because of this: I had dinner with Reid back in 2005, because we were a competitor of LinkedIn and I thought it would be interesting to sit down and compare notes. So I set up a meeting, and we had dinner in California — Silicon Valley or San Francisco, I don't remember exactly. And we started comparing notes. He basically said to me: "What you're doing is really interesting, but we want to dominate the social network for business professionals. That's our goal, and I'm going to acquire every relevant piece of it and raise as much money as possible."

I didn't know how well-connected he was at the time, so it wasn't hard for him to raise $155 million. And he said: "I couldn't care less about profitability — it's irrelevant for us. We are going to dominate that market space, and I'm just going to keep raising money to do it." Just to contrast — with Zoom, we reached profitability on $3 million. So both business models worked really well — at least for me and for him — but you can see the stark difference. He needed a lot of money to accomplish what he wanted to accomplish.

And in the end, he sold LinkedIn to Microsoft for $26 billion. Poor guy — my heart goes out to him. I went to check how much stock he still held at the time of the IPO — he had close to 30% of the company even after raising that $155 million. So the poor guy is not that poor.

So just to come back to our objectives and vision: we want to increase success rates. And now you see that the success rate for these kinds of business models — in my mind — is not 1 in 10, it's 1 in 100. And we want to be profitable. And with these models, that's just not straightforward.
When they went to the IPO, he had, I think, close to 30% of the company still after the $155 million. So the poor guy is not poor.

So just to go back to our objectives and vision — we want to increase success rates. And now you see that the success rate of these kinds of business models is not 1 out of 10; in my mind it's 1 out of 100. And we want it to be profitable. And it's just not working.

With these kinds of scalable business models, it's very difficult to do. So what do we do? Here it is. This is something I learned when talking to one venture capitalist. He came up with this VC ratio. So what is the VC ratio? It stands not for VC venture capital, but V is value at the exit and C is capital invested. So if you take what did you get for your investment — that's what he called the VC ratio. I thought it was really cute. His name is Jeroen. A company that raised $30 million and was sold for $300 million has a VC ratio of 10. You can check me — 300 divided by 30 is still 10. Not many companies are sold for $300 million. כשנכנסתי לעסקים בשנת 1982, '83, '84 — אני לא זוכר בדיוק — רצינו משהו לניהול מכירות. היה product שנקרא ACT! עם סימן קריאה בסוף. זה היה pre-CRM; זה בעצם Outlook. זה היה הכלי הראשון. ובאותה תקופה כבר היה CRM — אני לא זוכר את השם, החברה נמכרה ל-Oracle מאוחר יותר. נכון. תודה. הם מכרו את זה ל-Oracle. אף אחד לא ידע על זה, אף אחד לא הבין את זה. זו הייתה טכנולוגיה מסתורית שמה שחברות גדולות עשו איתה. וזה היה מ-'85 עד עכשיו — אז זה 40 שנה. לוקח הרבה זמן לפני ש-CRM מובן היטב וכל חברה יודעת שהיא צריכה אותו. לוקח זמן. ומה שאתם צריכים כחברה הוא זמן.

אוקיי, בוא נדבר קצת על מה שהולך לקרות בהמשך. לא תכננתי שיהיו 15 הרצאות — תכננתי שיהיו 13. אבל מה שקורה הוא שאנחנו מדברים עם יזמים כל הזמן, מדברים עם הרבה אנשים כל הזמן. וכשאני שומע משהו או רואה משהו ואני אומר, "זה פונדמנטלי" — כמו scalability. כשאנשים אומרים, "אוה, זה לא scalable, אנחנו לא יכולים לעשות את זה" — אז אני חושב שכדאי לבנות מצגת סביב זה וללכת לפרטים של מה זה בעצם אומר.

הזכרתי כמה דברים בפגישה. אני לא בטוח שאני הולך להפוך אותם להרצאה שלמה. אבל מכיוון שזה הרבה כיף, לפחות בשבילי — ובתקווה בשבילכם — יש סיכוי טוב שאחזור עם משהו מעניין. וכפי שהייתם כל כך אדיבים לומר לי, גם אם אני חוזר על עצמי, זה בסדר, כי אתם לא זוכרים כלום. נכון? זה היה מאוד אדיב מצדכם. אני גם לא זוכר, אבל אני יכול להסתכל על השקפים ולומר, "אלוהים, כבר אמרתי את זה."

אז יש סיכוי טוב שנשלח לכם email בעוד שבועיים-שלושה ונגיד, כן, יש לנו הרצאה נוספת. ואם לא, אתם תמיד מוזמנים לבוא ולדבר איתנו. תודה.

Lecture 15 of the SmartUp Foundations Course, delivered by Yonatan Stern, centres on one of the most misunderstood concepts in the startup world: scalability. The session challenges the conventional wisdom promoted by venture capital firms and argues that a blind pursuit of scalable business models is one of the primary reasons so many startups fail.

Stern opens by reframing SmartUp's core mission. With nine out of ten startups failing, the programme exists not merely to celebrate the rare success, but to dramatically improve the odds — ideally from one in ten to one in two or three. SmartUp defines a successful company as one that is consistently profitable, fast-growing, and built on a modest investment of roughly two to five million dollars, rather than the thirty to fifty million that VCs typically deploy. By increasing success rates and reducing capital requirements simultaneously, Stern argues the startup ecosystem could grow by a factor of ten — a vision he describes as an "infinite game" worth pursuing.

The lecture's central argument is that scalability, while a legitimate concept — meaning the ability to grow revenues without proportionally growing costs — has become a harmful filter in the hands of investors. VCs routinely reject sound business ideas simply because they appear non-scalable, dismissing services businesses, manual processes, or niche markets without properly understanding their strategic value. Stern contends this is a fundamental error. Non-scalable methods, used intelligently, are often the most effective way for an early-stage company to reach customers, generate real revenue, and build the market understanding needed to eventually scale.

He illustrates this through two case studies. The first is Bioform Beyond Data, a company converting clinical trial data to the SDTM standard. Rather than waiting for their software product to be ready, Stern guided the team to continue delivering results as a service, using their developing technology internally to improve margins. This kept them alive, generated nearly two million dollars in projected 2025 revenue, and gave them real-world data to refine their AI-driven product as the technology landscape evolved. The second example involves a company building tools to repurpose webinar content from YouTube — automatically identifying relevant business videos, processing them, and delivering value directly to marketing teams. Early results show high email open rates but low response rates, a reminder that market penetration takes iteration and time.

The unifying insight is that startups need what Stern calls "growth engines" — low-cost, self-funding mechanisms to stay present in a market while learning from real customers. Technology adoption, he notes, routinely takes decades, and what kills most startups is not a bad idea but a lack of time caused by misallocated capital and unrealistic expectations. The path to building a large company is gradual, grounded, and often begins with methods that no VC would fund.

ההרצאה עוסקת באסטרטגיה יזמית פרקטית, ומציגה כיצד חברה בתחום תכנון שרשרת האספקה (S&OP) בנתה מנוע צמיחה שיטתי על ידי הפיכת אתגרי שוק להזדמנויות עסקיות.

נקודת המוצא המרכזית של ההרצאה היא שהשוק לרוב אינו בשל למוצר חדש, ועל כן הגישה הישירה של מכירה חזיתית נכשלת. הפתרון שהוצג הוא שימוש בקורסי הכשרה כשלב ראשון בצינור המכירות. קורסים אלה אינם מאיימים על הלקוח הפוטנציאלי — הוא מקבל דיפלומה, מרגיש בטוח ביחס לביטחון תעסוקתי, ופתוח יותר לשמוע ולשתף בבעיות הארגוניות. כך נוצרת מערכת יחסים שבה הלקוח רואה בחברה מומחה ולא איש מכירות, לעיתים אף בהתרגשות אמיתית. עלות הקורס עמדה על כ-2,500 שקל לאדם, וכחצי מהמשתתפים ביקשו פגישת היכרות המשך.

השלב השני בצינור הוא תוכנית ניתוח ערך (VAP — Value Analysis Program), המחליפה את מחזור המכירות הארוך המסורתי הכולל proof of concept חינמי. במקום זאת, החברה גובה כ-7,200 דולר עבור ניתוח מעמיק ומוצג ללקוח כשירות בעל ערך עצמאי. הכנסות החברה בשנה השנייה לפעילותה הגיעו לכמעט חצי מיליון דולר — מבלי שהמוצר הטכנולוגי המרכזי נמכר בהיקפים משמעותיים.

ההרצאה מדגישה את העיקרון שלפיו בעיות הן הזדמנויות. כל מעבר לשלב חדש — מייעוץ ל-maturity assessment מקוון, ומשם ל-Agile S&OP פשוט שעוקב אחר פגישות ומסמכים — נבע מכישלון קודם שנבחן מחדש. לדוגמה, כשניסיון ה-maturity assessment המקוון לא ייצר המרות למרות open rate גבוה מאוד, הצוות פנה לפיתוח תוכן מסביר שמציב את החברה כ-thought leader בתחום.

לחיזוק הנקודה על scalability, הוצגה דוגמה מהניסיון האישי של המרצה עם CardScan בשנות התשעים — מוצר שגרר עלויות תמיכה טכנית בלתי-ניתנות-לקנה-מידה, ונפתר על ידי בניית קו תמיכה מובנה בן שלבים עם תגובה תוך 30 שניות. גם מוצר Pitch Video הוצג כמקרה בו השוק הסמוך — חברות עם תוכן וידאו קבור ב-YouTube — עשוי להיות פורה יותר מהשוק הישיר.

המסר המרכזי הוא שיזמים חייבים להישאר בשוק, לייצר הכנסה לאורך הדרך, ולהתקדם בהדרגה. הגישה הפרקטית אינה מנוגדת לחזון — להיפך, היא מה שמאפשר לעצב אותו ביחס למציאות שבה לקוחות קונים ומשתמשים.
